title: Verifier‑Grounded Evaluation of LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: A Preregistered NetConfig‑Semantic Study
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1; preregistration SHA‑256 7db1663cf3982c8ea1e16c3dd7c0348f356bb4cbe3978ecc75bb59fdedb71a37) that compared a deterministic template baseline to a single‑pass LLM generator (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini) on N = 120 synthetic intent→configuration tasks using a deterministic validator. Under the frozen confirmatory semantics (shared_initial_candidate per pair) all confirmatory episodes completed: baseline = 120/120 verifier passes; guarded (gpt‑5‑mini, seed_0) = 120/120 verifier passes. Paired difference = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We (i) publish the exact execution and analysis artifacts and SHA‑256 fingerprints needed to reproduce the run, (ii) diagnose—using the archived artifacts—why the paired outcome is uninformative about independent generative reliability (shared_initial_candidate design, template‑tight task synthesis, and validator–task coupling), and (iii) provide artifact‑grounded, runnable experimental modifications (independent_per_condition sampling, multi‑seed confirmatory design, validator diversity, task heterogeneity) that produce informative independent comparisons. The immutable initial master prompt is archived (provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba).

sections.introduction:
Automating NetOps by mapping natural‑language intent to device configuration is an active research and production goal. Generative large language models (LLMs) can reduce operator effort and accelerate provisioning but raise safety‑critical questions about semantic correctness: reachability, access‑control preservation, ordering constraints, and transient safety during multi‑step changes. Prior engineering work shows the operational utility of verifier grounding for pre‑deployment checks (e.g., Batfish) and the general need to measure semantic correctness with deterministic analyzers [https://doi.org/10.1145/3603269.3604866].

We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory experiment whose purpose was operationally precise: compare a deterministic template baseline to a guarded LLM pipeline (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini) using a verifier as the objective correctness oracle. The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1; SHA‑256 7db1663cf3...) and the immutable master prompt (provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 1872df1e...) are archived and form part of the mandatory Disclosure (see Disclosure). Our design intentionally emphasized deterministic reproducibility: (1) synthetic tasks were programmatically generated from deterministic templates with explicit required_sequences and workflow_policies, (2) a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) evaluated candidate configurations and produced full scoring traces, and (3) complete execution artifacts and SHA‑256 fingerprints were archived to permit exact auditing and reruns. 

The confirmatory estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline over N = 120 tasks. Below we report the exact archived numerical outcomes, provide representative artifact evidence, analyze why the observed paired result is degenerate under the preregistered semantics, and give concrete, artifact‑grounded changes that produce informative independent comparisons while preserving reproducibility.
sections.related_work:
Verifier‑centric NetOps evaluation. Tools that compute network control‑plane and data‑plane behavior offline (Batfish and successors) demonstrate that semantic validators materially improve pre‑deployment confidence and prevent outages [https://doi.org/10.1145/3603269.3604866]. Recent LLM→NetOps literature focuses on intent translation, template synthesis, or generate–validate–repair loops; authors emphasize that token/fluency metrics poorly reflect operational correctness and advocate verifier‑based evaluation frameworks [https://doi.org/10.23919/cnsm62983.2024.10814407, https://doi.org/10.1002/nem.70029].

Methodological gap and our positioning. Many prior evaluations either (A) report model‑level metrics without deterministic validators, or (B) run generate–validate pipelines but do not preregister confirmatory estimands or fully publish execution manifests. We contribute a complementary artifact‑anchored protocol: a frozen preregistration, deterministic validator traces per episode, full per‑file SHA‑256 manifest, and a complete reproducible run (see execution/execution_manifest.json). The packaged artifacts enable exact reproduction and immediate surgical reruns under alternative, informative generation semantics.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration summary. The preregistered study CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1 (SHA‑256 7db1663cf3...) specified (i) a paired confirmatory test (H1): paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline over N = 120 tasks (40 per topology class: edge, datacenter, multi‑AS), (ii) primary analysis = paired_binary_analysis_v1 with 10,000 bootstrap resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) for CI, and (iii) confirmatory generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (one canonical candidate per pair supplied to both baseline and guarded episodes). The preregistration also declared exploratory follow‑ups (seed sensitivity, rank stability) and an explicit retry and missingness policy.

Task generation, constraints, and validators. Tasks were generated deterministically from a template bank (generator_id = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5, version 5.0). Each task manifest entry contains: initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence (canonical step sequence), workflow_policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, minimum_active_in_groups), and allowed_touched_fields. Representative entries and per‑task payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl. The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, version 5.0) enforces parsed command counts, explicit intent constraints, transient safety checks, and emits normalized configurations and validator traces. Per‑episode scoring JSONs live at execution/scoring/*.json (example SHA‑256s in the execution manifest). The choice of a deterministic, constraint‑aware validator was deliberate: it maximizes interpretability of pass/fail outcomes and supports exact reproducibility.

Model, adapter, and execution contract. Declared LLM = gpt‑5‑mini accessed via provider adapter 'openai_responses' using the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family. Model configuration and adapter settings are archived at execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da...). The execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) records: planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, model_calls_used = 120, failed_episode_count = 0, and per‑file SHA‑256s for all responses, scoring JSONs, and provider call traces. Contamination detection (exact‑match and 5‑gram overlap thresholds) was executed per preregistered rules; the summary file analysis/contamination_summary.csv is archived.

Confirmatory generation semantics and rationale. The preregistered confirmatory semantics 'shared_initial_candidate' was selected to remove generation variability as a confound in the comparison of validator treatment across conditions: for each pair a single canonical candidate (seed_0) is produced and then presented to both the deterministic template baseline and to the guarded LLM condition for scoring. This isolates scoring/validator differences at the cost of suppressing independent generative variability. The shared candidate files and provider traces are archived at execution/responses/*-shared-initial.txt and execution/provider_calls/*-shared-initial.json and are referenced in the Disclosure Statement.
sections.results:
Execution and raw outcomes. All preregistered confirmatory episodes completed without infrastructure failures (complete_pair_count = 120). The archived confirmatory counts are:
- baseline_success_count = 120/120 (baseline pass rate = 1.00)
- guarded_success_count = 120/120 (gpt‑5‑mini pass rate = 1.00)
The paired contingency table is degenerate: n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 9f25790c...). The primary estimator (mean of guarded_i − baseline_i across tasks) = 0.00.

Inference under the preregistered analysis. Following the frozen analysis plan we computed a 95% bootstrap percentile CI for the paired difference with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). The CI is [0.00, 0.00] and the exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. The analysis artifacts are archived (analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Representative scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task‑000001‑guarded.json SHA‑256 0d56c1ad...) show parsed_command_count and validator final_state details for inspected tasks.

Representative artifact evidence. Example pair pair‑000001 (task‑000001): the shared_initial candidate (execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt; SHA‑256 8f38c8be...) is identical to both the deterministic template baseline and the guarded LLM responses in the archived outputs. The validator trace for task‑000001 shows parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, violation_count = 0 and final_state matching the task's expected_final_state (see execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json). Similar identicalities occur across the published representative pairs (task‑000002, task‑000003, etc.). The provider call audit in deterministic_reconciliation.json records hosted_model_call_event_count = 120 and cache_miss_count = 120.

Contamination and quality checks. The preregistered contamination heuristics applied to confirmatory candidates flagged no items under the pre‑specified thresholds; the contamination summary (analysis/contamination_summary.csv) contains no confirmatory flags. The full per‑file SHA‑256 manifest is included in the execution bundle to permit byte‑level verification of every referenced artifact.
sections.discussion:
Why the paired outcome is uninformative about independent generative reliability. The archived artifacts support a clear, artifact‑grounded causal account: (A) shared_initial_candidate semantics produced a single canonical candidate per pair that was used by both conditions (evidence: execution/responses/*-shared-initial.txt and execution/provider_calls/*-shared-initial.json), (B) the task templates encoded deterministic required_sequences and tight workflow_policies (evidence: execution/task_manifest.jsonl entries with required_sequence and must_be_down_for_fields), and (C) the deterministic validator enforces these template constraints (evidence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 traces in execution/scoring/*.json). When an identical canonical candidate satisfies template constraints, both baseline and guarded episodes necessarily receive the same validator judgement, producing n_11 = N. Thus the confirmatory paired test, as preregistered, measured whether the validator treats an identical artifact differently across conditions (it did not) rather than measuring independent model reliability under stochastic generation.

Operational implications. For operational evaluation of LLM‑driven NetOps automation the relevant question is independent generative reliability under realistic sampling and prompt/seed variability. A confirmatory design that supplies independent candidates per condition (independent_per_condition) or multi‑seed confirmatory replication is required to test whether LLM generation yields different verifier pass probabilities than templates. The archived bundle supports immediate reruns under these alternative semantics without code invention: change the generation adapter to produce independent candidates per condition or to emit multiple confirmatory seeds, then re‑score using the same deterministic validator. All artifacts and hashes required for such reruns are published (see execution_manifest.json).

Runnable corrective experimental modifications (artifact‑grounded). Using the released artifacts one can: (1) switch to independent_per_condition confirmatory sampling (produce one candidate per condition per pair and re‑run scoring); (2) adopt multi‑seed confirmatory design (treat seeds_0..K as confirmatory replicates and aggregate within‑condition pass probabilities); (3) diversify validators (add a second validator—e.g., a reachability/emulation analyzer—and report intersection/union pass rates to reduce validator–task coupling); and (4) broaden task heterogeneity (expand template bank with paraphrase variants and randomized workflow_policies). Each modification requires only edits to the generation configuration and re‑execution using the same scoring harness; exact file paths and invocation traces for the original run are archived to accelerate reruns.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: preregistered shared_initial design intentionally limited per‑pair variability and therefore reduced scope for independent generative claims. Construct validity: deterministic validators enforce template constraints and may overstate performance relative to open‑distribution operational intents. External validity: we evaluated a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and synthetic template tasks; results do not generalize across model families or real operational intent distributions. Conclusion validity: the degenerate contingency yields trivial statistical outputs that are arithmetically correct but substantively uninformative about independent generation reliability.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, verifier‑grounded paired experiment and publicly released a complete artifact bundle enabling exact reproduction (execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/*). Under the preregistered confirmatory semantics (shared_initial_candidate) both the deterministic template baseline and the gpt‑5‑mini guarded condition validated on all N = 120 tasks (both 120/120). Archival evidence (shared_initial candidate files and validator scoring traces) shows that identical canonical candidates per pair and template‑tight task constraints caused the degenerate paired outcome. Consequently, the confirmatory paired result does not provide evidence about independent LLM generative reliability in operational settings. We provide artifact‑grounded, runnable modifications (independent_per_condition sampling, multi‑seed confirmatory execution, validator diversification, task heterogeneity) that preserve reproducibility and produce informative independent comparisons. All cited execution and analysis artifacts—including the immutable master prompt reference (provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) and the preregistration SHA‑256—are included in the submission bundle to permit exact audit and follow‑up experiments.

limitations: Controlled synthetic tasks: programmatic templates produced narrow required_sequences and workflow_policies that favour canonical solutions and limit external generalizability to heterogeneous operational intents.

Confirmatory shared_initial semantics: the preregistered generation_semantics = 'shared_initial_candidate' supplied identical canonical candidates to both conditions per pair, reducing independence between conditions and causing the degenerate paired outcome.

Single canonical seed for confirmatory test: the primary analysis used one canonical seed per task; preregistered exploratory multi‑seed analyses (seeds_1..4) were not included in the confirmatory inference reported here.

Validator–task coupling: the deterministic validator enforces constraints encoded in the task templates, which can increase pass rates for template‑aligned candidates and reduce construct validity for open distributions.

Possible training‑data exposure: preregistered contamination heuristics found no flags under chosen thresholds, but absence of a flag is not proof of zero exposure to related artifacts in model pretraining.

Single‑model, single‑validator run: results apply only to gpt‑5‑mini under the recorded configuration and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; they do not generalize across model families, agentic pipelines, or other validators.
